The American Automotive Policy Council urged the U.S. and Dutch governments to accelerate negotiations on Nexperia’s export restrictions, warning that prolonged uncertainty could disrupt chip supplies for mid-size gasoline vehicles. Ford announced it will temporarily prioritize production of its best-selling gasoline-powered F-Series trucks while seeking alternative aluminum suppliers after the Novelis mill fire disrupted 40% of U.S. automotive sheet supply. On October 23, 2025, the German automotive industry association VDA urged the European Commission to intervene in the escalating chip supply dispute involving Nexperia, warning that without a diplomatic solution, production lines at several European automakers could face partial stoppages within weeks. The European Automobile Manufacturers' Association repeated its call for immediate talks, noting that Nexperia's stocks for basic automotive chips may last only a few more days industry-wide.

BMW said it is doubling down on local chip sourcing for its China operations, following Volkswagen’s in-house assisted driving chip announcement. CEO Oliver Zipse told a German business daily that the company plans to partner with a Chinese semiconductor firm to secure supply for its next-generation electric models, aiming to reduce reliance on Nexperia and hedge against further export disruptions under the ongoing U.S.-China trade tensions. BMW declined to comment on production adjustments at its North American plants.

German automakers reported that the short-term special export permits for China-owned Nexperia chips are being granted on a wider basis, following Volkswagen’s initial deliveries. BMW and Mercedes-Benz confirmed they have received limited shipments to maintain critical production lines. However, industry executives cautioned that the case-by-case approval system offers no guarantee of stable supply, and that the one-year U.S. waiver could still be revoked amid shifts in trade negotiations. Simultaneously, Honda announced it will accelerate its shift of small-car production to India, targeting 200,000 annual capacity by 2027 to bypass tariff-hit Mexican and Southeast Asian operations. Honda announced plans to establish a new production hub in India to offset tariff impacts and chip supply disruptions. Honda's executive said the India expansion would begin with a new assembly line for the sedan segment, aiming to serve both local and export markets. The move is part of a broader strategy to regain lost market share in Southeast Asia, where Chinese EV makers have eroded sales. Analysts noted that India's lower labor costs and trade policies make it an attractive alternative, but cautioned that the shift will take time and investment.

The German automaker urged the European Union to press for a permanent diplomatic framework ensuring predictable chip exports from China. The Japanese carmaker said it would invest in alternative chip sources in Taiwan and the United States to reduce reliance on Chinese-controlled production. Honda, still grappling with its profit warning, confirmed it had no immediate plans to adjust its Asia output despite the ongoing shortage. The broader automotive sector faces continued uncertainty as trade tensions persist.

German auto industry representatives urged the European Commission to press China for equal access to streamlined rare-earth export licenses, arguing that preferential treatment for U.S. customers violates World Trade Organization principles and threatens the competitiveness of European automakers.
